location.mountain: Wuyi Mountains, Niaoshidian and Malin areas

description.short: Spicy, cinnamon-scented rock oolong — one of the most iconic and beloved teas of Wuyishan
description.overview: Alongside Shui Xian, Rou Gui forms one half of the foundational pillar of Wuyi rock tea, celebrated for its pungent cinnamon spice, robust body, and fierce rock rhyme.
description.leaf: Large, dark-brown, tightly twisted leaves with roasted gleam
description.liquor: Rich orange-red to bright amber infusion
description.aroma: Cinnamon bark, warm spices, subtle sweetness, and deep stony minerality
description.taste: Spicy with an assertive cinnamon note, full-bodied, mineral, accompanied by a dry, structured finish
description.aftertaste: Long, spicy-sweet, leaving a warming glow in the throat
description.processing: Plucking → solar withering → vigorous tossing/bruising for pronounced edge oxidation → fixation (kill-green) → rolling → multi-stage charcoal roasting

history.origin: The name translates to 'Cassia' or 'Cinnamon', derived from its distinctively sharp, spicy aroma reminiscent of Chinese cassia bark.
history.development: Recorded in the Wuyi region since the Qing dynasty (19th century), it surged in prominence in the late 20th century to become the flagship export and benchmark of Wuyi Yancha.
history.modern: Today, Rou Gui from prestigious micro-terroirs commands cult status and premium prices for its exceptional intensity and 'rock rhyme' (yan yun).
interestingFacts: Rou Gui is prized as sharper, spicier, and more aggressive compared to the softer, woody Shui Xian; tea masters often brew them back-to-back as the twin archetypes of Wuyi oolongs.
Roasting levels for Rou Gui vary significantly from medium floral-spicy to deep charcoal-roasted, dramatically shifting its aromatic expression.
